correctness.rationale: The complete \(2\times2\) and \(3\times3\) profile spaces are exhausted. Two DA implementations agree; stability and student-optimality are checked against every stable perfect assignment; direct Pareto comparisons agree with an independent trading-cycle test; and the priority-level zero-inefficiency classification agrees exactly with a direct Ergin-cycle test. The resulting counts and uniqueness claims use exact finite comparisons only.

evidence: Ergin establishes acyclicity as the relevant priority condition for efficiency of the priority-respecting rule.

Klaus-Klijn give a full-text definition of Ergin cycles and state that with unit quotas the cycle condition alone suffices; they restate the unique fair-and-efficient DA-based mechanism result without couples.
Narita shows that the original proof needs correction but that Ergin's theorem itself remains valid.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These sources supply broader qualitative structure but no exact enumeration of the \(3\times3\) domain. The accepted counts are therefore not implied without a separate finite classification.

originality.rationale: The qualitative Ergin acyclicity theorem is prior and explicitly excluded from novelty. The inspected primary literature does not state the exact three-student profile incidence, the priority-structure frequency histogram, the assigned-rank split, or the unique two-student repair structure.
residual_risks: An alternative bibliographic DOI appears in some secondary databases for the 2002 Ergin article; the publisher DOI is used in this package.
An unindexed note, thesis, classroom enumeration, or code archive may contain the same exact small-market counts.

The original Ergin full text was not obtained in this run; the theorem and unit-quota cycle definition were checked in later open full-text primary literature, and the 2021 corrigendum confirms the theorem remains valid.
No larger-market frequency claim is made.

value.rationale: Student-proposing deferred acceptance and Ergin acyclicity are central objects in priority-based allocation. Three students is the smallest size where cyclic priorities can cause Pareto inefficiency. The exact first-size incidence, priority histogram, and unique two-student repair structure give a natural quantitative refinement of the qualitative efficiency theorem.
